metadata.summary: This issue contains separate clinical articles rather than a single practice guideline. It discusses updates to microscopic hematuria and male chronic pelvic pain guidelines alongside articles on stone procedures, prostate cancer, intravesical bladder cancer treatments, and socioeconomic factors associated with urinary stone risk. It also describes the design of the SOUL trial; the trial's proposed outcomes are not presented as established findings.

therapies_index.name: α blockers
therapies_index.administration: Oral treatment; described as most suitable for men with pain and obstructive voiding symptoms.

therapies_index.name: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications
therapies_index.administration: Used as part of multimodal treatment for chronic pelvic pain.

therapies_index.administration: Used as medication for neuropathic pain in chronic pelvic pain treatment.

therapies_index.administration: Used as medication for neuropathic pain in chronic pelvic pain treatment.

therapies_index.name: pregabalin
therapies_index.administration: Used as medication for neuropathic pain in chronic pelvic pain treatment.

therapies_index.name: antibiotics
therapies_index.administration: For CP/CPPS, use is limited to patients with a positive culture; an empiric 4- or 6-week course is not recommended. A single short empiric course of 10days is considered reasonable for chronic orchialgia.

therapies_index.name: tadalafil
therapies_index.administration: Daily treatment for CPPS, with or without erectile dysfunction.

therapies_index.name: pelvic floor physical therapy
therapies_index.administration: For men with PFM or abdominopelvic muscle myalgia, referral to a therapist with specialized pelvic-floor training is described as part of multimodal care.

therapies_index.name: myofascial release
therapies_index.administration: A therapeutic technique offered during pelvic floor physical therapy.

therapies_index.name: biofeedback
therapies_index.mechanism: Intended to reduce resting pelvic muscle tone.
therapies_index.administration: A therapeutic technique offered during pelvic floor physical therapy.

therapies_index.name: cognitive behavior therapy
therapies_index.administration: Described as part of a multimodal approach to coping and stress management.

therapies_index.name: guided meditation
therapies_index.administration: Used as a relaxation technique.

therapies_index.name: diaphragmatic breathing exercises
therapies_index.administration: Used as a relaxation technique.

therapies_index.name: extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL)
therapies_index.administration: Studies applied low-intensity ESWL over 2 to 12 weeks for CPPS; the article states that this indication remains off label.

therapies_index.name: spermatic cord block
therapies_index.administration: Used diagnostically for isolated orchialgia; temporary pain relief and a favorable response can help identify potential benefit from MSDSC.

therapies_index.name: microsurgical denervation of the spermatic cord (MSDSC)
therapies_index.administration: A targeted approach divides the cremasteric muscle fibers, peri-vasal sheath and lipomatous area of the posterior spermatic cord while preserving the vas deferens and lymphatic vessels.

therapies_index.name: vasovasostomy
therapies_index.administration: Described by expert opinion as an option for postvasectomy pain syndrome.

therapies_index.name: epididymectomy
therapies_index.administration: Described by expert opinion as an option for postvasectomy pain syndrome.

therapies_index.name: inguinal orchiectomy
therapies_index.administration: May be considered as a last resort after conservative treatments and less-invasive operations fail.

therapies_index.name: ureteroscopy
therapies_index.administration: Used to treat upper urinary tract stones; a temporary ureteral stent may be placed afterward or omitted following an uncomplicated procedure.

therapies_index.name: ureteral stent
therapies_index.mechanism: Temporary placement can facilitate renal drainage and prevent pain related to ureteral trauma or obstructing fragments.
therapies_index.administration: May be placed after ureteroscopy; AUA guidance cited in the article permits omission after uncomplicated ureteroscopy.
key_toxicities: The Michigan Urological Surgery Improvement Collaborative found that placement increased the odds of a postoperative emergency department visit after ureteroscopy by 25%; many visits involved pain, urinary discomfort or hematuria.

therapies_index.name: laser lithotripsy
therapies_index.administration: Used to fragment stones during ureteroscopic treatment, including procedures employing aspiration technologies.

therapies_index.name: percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
therapies_index.administration: Described as the gold standard for stones > 2 cm according to many guidelines.

therapies_index.name: direct in-scope suction (DISS)
therapies_index.mechanism: Alternating suction through a ureteroscope removes stone fragments or dust during or after laser lithotripsy.
therapies_index.administration: Two 3-way stopcock adapters connect the ureteroscope irrigation channel to suction and irrigation tubing.

therapies_index.name: flexible and navigable (FANS) suction ureteral access sheath
therapies_index.mechanism: A steerable vacuum-assisted sheath reaches different calyces to aspirate stone fragments and dust directly.
therapies_index.administration: Used during vacuum-assisted ureteroscopic stone removal.

therapies_index.name: steerable ureteroscopic renal evacuation (SURE)
therapies_index.mechanism: The CVAC System combines endoscopic visualization, laser lithotripsy, irrigation and aspiration to evacuate stone fragments.
therapies_index.administration: Performed with the single-use CVAC System to access the renal collecting system.

therapies_index.name: CVAC System
therapies_index.mechanism: Its separate irrigation and vacuum channels provide continuous flow for removal of dust and stone fragments during and after laser lithotripsy.
therapies_index.administration: Single-use aspiration system integrated with a ureteroscope for SURE.

therapies_index.name: basket extraction
therapies_index.administration: Described as a stone-extraction comparator after laser lithotripsy.

therapies_index.name: testosterone therapy (TTh)
therapies_index.administration: Discussed for carefully selected men with hypogonadism after definitive treatment of localized prostate cancer and for selected men undergoing active surveillance.
monitoring: Monitor PSA velocity and testosterone levels regularly in men receiving TTh after prostate cancer treatment.

therapies_index.name: Nadofaragene firadenovec
therapies_index.mechanism: A nonreplicating adenoviral vector delivers the interferon alfa-2b gene to the bladder urothelium.
approved_indications: FDA-approved following a trial in BCG-unresponsive HR NMIBC with CIS ± papillary disease.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical single 75 mL dose every 3 mo.

therapies_index.name: Nogapendekin alfa-inbakicept
therapies_index.mechanism: An IL-15 receptor agonist that activates natural killer and CD8+ T cells when given with BCG.
therapies_index.administration: Given concurrently with BCG.

therapies_index.name: BCG
therapies_index.administration: Described as intravesical treatment, including induction and maintenance schedules and combinations with other agents.

therapies_index.name: NAI + BCG
therapies_index.mechanism: Nogapendekin alfa-inbakicept activates natural killer and CD8+ T cells to augment the response to BCG.
approved_indications: FDA-approved in April 2024 following the QUILT 3.032 trial in BCG-unresponsive NMIBC.
therapies_index.administration: Induction: every wk x6; maintenance: every wk x3 at 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18 mo.

therapies_index.name: Cretostimogene grenadenorepvec (CG0070)
therapies_index.mechanism: An oncolytic adenovirus directed at tumor cells with a defective Rb pathway that also expresses granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical induction every wk x6; maintenance every wk x3 every 3 mo, as listed for Cretostimogene (CG0070).
key_toxicities: The BOND003 cohort C update reported no grade 3 or greater treatment-related AEs.

therapies_index.name: TAR-200
therapies_index.mechanism: An intravesical device provides sustained gemcitabine release over weeks.
therapies_index.administration: Placed through a urethral catheter; every 3 wk for 24 wk, then every 12 wk until wk 96.

therapies_index.name: gemcitabine
therapies_index.administration: Delivered intravesically by TAR-200 or sequentially with docetaxel in Gem/Doce.

therapies_index.name: TAR-200 + cetrelimab
therapies_index.administration: Investigated in SunRISe-1 cohort 1.

therapies_index.name: TAR-210
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses the TAR-200 platform to deliver erdafitinib directly to the bladder.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical treatment every 12 wk in the comparison table; MoonRISE-1 compares administration every-3months with intravesical chemotherapy.

therapies_index.name: erdafitinib
therapies_index.administration: Delivered directly to the bladder by TAR-210 in patients with FGFR3-mutant NMIBC.

therapies_index.name: sasanlimab
therapies_index.mechanism: An anti-PD-1 antibody providing systemic immune activation.
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous treatment every 4 wk in the combination schedule listed in the table.

therapies_index.name: Sasanlimab + BCG
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines systemic immune activation from sasanlimab with BCG treatment.
therapies_index.administration: BCG induction every wk x6; sasanlimab subcutaneous every 4 wk; BCG maintenance every wk x3 every 3 mo.

therapies_index.name: EG-70 (detalimogene voraplasmid)
therapies_index.mechanism: A nonviral, nonintegrating intravesical immunotherapy designed to induce a local antitumor immune response.
therapies_index.administration: Every 3 wk x4, as listed for Detalimogene (EG-70).
key_toxicities: Reported treatment-related AEs were mostly grade 1 to 2 and consistent with catheterization and instillation.

therapies_index.name: TARA-002
therapies_index.mechanism: An immune-stimulatory agent derived from OK-432.
therapies_index.administration: Every wk x6 in the comparison table.
key_toxicities: The article reports no grade ≥ 3 treatment-related AEs.

therapies_index.name: Gem/Doce
therapies_index.administration: Sequential intravesical treatment; induction every wk x6 and maintenance every mo x24 in the comparison table.

therapies_index.name: docetaxel
therapies_index.administration: Administered sequentially with intravesical gemcitabine as Gem/Doce.

conditions.name: microscopic hematuria (MH)
conditions.description: The AUA evaluation approach assigns patients to malignancy-risk groups so that the intensity of investigation reflects their risk.
conditions.epidemiology: MH is common, whereas an underlying malignancy is uncommon. Studies cited for the 2020 low-risk group reported cancer detection of 0.0% to 0.4%.

subtypes.name: Low/Negligible
subtypes.distinguishing_features: All low/negligible-risk criteria must be met; the table reports a malignancy risk of 0-0.4%.

subtypes.name: Intermediate
subtypes.distinguishing_features: At least one intermediate-risk criterion is sufficient; the table reports a malignancy risk of 0.2-3.1%.

subtypes.name: High
subtypes.distinguishing_features: At least one high-risk criterion is sufficient; the table reports a malignancy risk of 1.3-6.3%. Age alone does not place women in this group.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify hematuria and determine whether it persists.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Repeat within 6 months for low/negligible-risk MH; use repeat results to guide subsequent risk-based evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A single UA showing 3-10 RBC/HPF, 11-25 RBC/HPF, or >25 RBC/HPF corresponds to a low/negligible-, intermediate-, or high-risk criterion, respectively. A previously low-risk patient without prior evaluation who has 3-25 RBC/HPF on repeat UA meets the table's alternative intermediate-risk criterion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Directly inspect for malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Part of the recommended intermediate-risk evaluation and the high-risk evaluation; perform it if MH persists after an intermediate-risk patient initially avoids cystoscopy on the basis of a urine test.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the upper urinary tract.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended alongside cystoscopy for intermediate-risk MH.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess malignancy risk when an intermediate-risk patient wishes to avoid cystoscopy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be offered after counseling about the risk of foregoing direct visualization; it should not determine the need for cystoscopy in low/negligible- or high-risk patients.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In an intermediate-risk patient, a negative UBTM/cytology reduces the estimated chance of detecting cancer to 0.1% to 0.4%. Several tests, including urine cytology, had reported NPV of 95% to 100% in the target population.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess malignancy risk when an intermediate-risk patient wishes to avoid cystoscopy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be offered after counseling about the risk of foregoing direct visualization; they should not determine the need for cystoscopy in low/negligible- or high-risk patients.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In an intermediate-risk patient, a negative UBTM/cytology reduces the estimated chance of detecting cancer to 0.1% to 0.4%. In a cited randomized trial, Cxbladder Triage had an NPV of 99%, and the marker-based approach reduced cystoscopy use by 59%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Visualize renal parenchyma and urothelium during upper-tract evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Remains the gold-standard imaging evaluation for high-risk MH in the discussion.

prognostic_tools.name: AUA MH risk stratification system
components: Degree of hematuria on a single urinalysis
Hematuria on repeat urinalysis in a previously low-risk patient without prior evaluation
Other risk factors for urothelial cancer

risk_groups.criteria: All listed low/negligible-risk criteria are required: 3-10 RBC/HPF on one urinalysis; women <60 years or men <40 years; never smoker or <10 pack years; and no other urothelial cancer risk factors.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The table gives a malignancy risk of 0-0.4%.

risk_groups.criteria: One or more listed criteria suffice: 11-25 RBC/HPF on one urinalysis; 3-25 RBC/HPF on repeat urinalysis in a previously low-risk patient without prior evaluation; women ≥60 years or men 40-59 years; 10-30 pack years; or one or more other urothelial cancer risk factors.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The table gives a malignancy risk of 0.2-3.1%.

risk_groups.criteria: One or more listed criteria suffice: >25 RBC/HPF on one urinalysis; a history of gross hematuria; men ≥60 years; >30 pack years; or one or more other urothelial cancer risk factors together with any high-risk feature. Women must not be placed in the high-risk group because of age alone.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The table gives a malignancy risk of 1.3-6.3%.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The malignancy-risk figures in the table derive from the 2020 AUA/Society for Urodynamics, Female Pelvic Medicine & Urogenital Reconstruction risk definition. The 2025 revision raises the age threshold used for low-risk women and removes age alone as a basis for assigning women to high risk.

follow_up.schedule: For low/negligible-risk MH, repeat UA within 6 months and offer risk-based evaluation if MH persists. For intermediate-risk patients who avoid cystoscopy on the basis of marker results, repeat UA within 12 months and perform cystoscopy if MH persists. After a negative risk-stratified evaluation, decide with the patient whether and when to repeat UA; most patients need no continuing urologic monitoring.
recommended_tests: cystoscopy if MH persists after an intermediate-risk patient initially forgoes it
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Cited studies found no increased risk of later cancer associated with a history of MH; subsequent cancer diagnoses after a negative evaluation were uncommon and occurred more than 3 years afterward.

conditions.name: chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS)
synonyms: NIH category III chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome
conditions.description: This male chronic pelvic pain diagnosis requires exclusion of other pathology. Pelvic floor myalgia or dysfunction commonly accompanies it.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pain may involve the perineum, testis, or penis and may accompany dysuria or painful ejaculation. Scrotal pain can occur alongside pain in other regions. Pain related to bladder filling and/or emptying instead points toward interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome.

conditions.name: upper urinary tract stones
conditions.description: The articles discuss renal and ureteral stones treated by ureteroscopy, aspiration-assisted approaches, or PCNL, and factors associated with stone recurrence.
conditions.epidemiology: Kidney stones affect 10% of the US population; approximately one-half of affected patients have a recurrence over a 10-year follow-up.

subtypes.name: calcium phosphate stone
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In the reported retrospective study, calcium phosphate stone analysis was significantly more likely in the most disadvantaged quartile measured by either ADI or DCI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify urine abnormalities relevant to recurrence risk and medical prevention.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The reported study assessed associations of socioeconomic indices with low urine volume, hypocitraturia, urinary uric acid, oxalate, hyperuricosuria, and hyperoxaluria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the type of stone.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The retrospective study reported an association between greater disadvantage by either ADI or DCI and calcium phosphate stone analysis.

prognostic_tools.name: Area Deprivation Index (ADI)
components: 17 variables from US Census data for geocoded residential addresses

risk_groups.criteria: Neighborhoods in the most disadvantaged ADI quartile in the reported study.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: Associated with younger age, higher BMI, non-White race, lower likelihood of completing a 24hU study, and significantly higher risk of low urine volume and calcium phosphate stone analysis.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: ADI assigns a neighborhood percentile score from 1 to 100, with 100 indicating the greatest disadvantage. In the reported study, increasing ADI, but not DCI, was associated with hypocitraturia.

prognostic_tools.name: Distressed Communities Index (DCI)
components: 7 variables using residential data at zip code level

risk_groups.criteria: Neighborhoods in the most disadvantaged DCI quartile in the reported study.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: Associated with younger age, higher BMI, non-White race, lower likelihood of completing a 24hU study, and significantly higher risk of low urine volume and calcium phosphate stone analysis.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: In the reported study, greater disadvantage by DCI was associated with lower urinary uric acid and oxalate, whereas improved socioeconomic status measured by DCI was associated with greater risk of hyperuricosuria and hyperoxaluria. Neither index fit better for 24hU outcomes for which both models were significant.

long_term_effects: Approximately one-half of patients with kidney stones experience recurrence over a 10-year follow-up.

artifacts.title: AUA/Society of Urodynamics, Female Pelvic Medicine & Urogenital Reconstruction microhematuria diagnostic algorithm
artifacts.description: Step 1: Classify microscopic hematuria using the risk categories in the stratification table. artifacts.title: Study workflow of the Stent Omission After Ureteroscopy and Lithotripsy (SOUL) combined randomized and observational clinical trial
artifacts.description: Step 1: Enroll eligible patients undergoing ureteroscopy and lithotripsy. Step 2: Patients accepting randomization enter the randomized cohort; at the end of lithotripsy, an intraoperative web-based assignment allocates stent placement or omission, provided they remain eligible. Patients declining randomization may enter an observational cohort, in which the surgeon determines stent use. Step 3: Obtain validated patient-reported outcome surveys and follow participants at 7 to 10 days and 4 to 6 weeks after the procedure. Step 4: From postoperative day 1 through 10, collect daily text-message assessments of pain, medication use and interference with activities; also collect time away from work or school.
artifacts.summary: The SOUL workflow accommodates both patients willing to be randomized and those choosing an observational pathway. It specifies when treatment allocation and subsequent patient-reported assessments occur.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The two-cohort design and timing of assignment are essential for interpreting future patient-centered outcomes of stent omission versus placement.

document_sections.heading: Microscopic Hematuria Guideline Amendment: Refined Risk Stratification and Introduction of Urinary Biomarkers
document_sections.content: The AUA revision of its microscopic hematuria (MH) guideline builds on changes since the initial 2012 publication. That version directed cystoscopy and CT urogram for every patient older than 35 years with any degree of MH. Because MH is common but an underlying malignancy is uncommon, this approach had substantial cost and low diagnostic yield. The 2020 guideline introduced risk stratification to match evaluation intensity to malignancy risk. The 2025 revision further adjusts that approach using evidence published in the interim.

document_sections.heading: Table. Risk Stratification
document_sections.content: The table sets out malignancy risk and the hematuria, age, smoking and other urothelial-cancer criteria for the Low/Negligible, Intermediate and High groups. The low-risk category was renamed low/negligible in recognition of its 0%-0.4% malignancy incidence. Under the revised approach, women < 60 years old without risk factors are low/negligible risk; women 60 years and older without other high-risk factors are intermediate risk. Age alone should no longer place women in the high-risk group, unlike the 2020 approach. The table’s malignancy estimates use the risk definitions of the 2020 AUA/Society for Urodynamics, Female Pelvic Medicine & Urogenital Reconstruction guideline; studies published subsequently found significantly lower urothelial-malignancy risk among women.

document_sections.heading: Low/Negligible Risk
document_sections.content: Sancı et al, Saxon et al and Woldu et al reported cancer detection of 0.0% to 0.4% in the 2020 low-risk group. The revised guideline recommends repeat urinalysis (UA) within 6 months rather than immediate evaluation. Previously, the recommendation was shared decision-making about repeat UA versus immediate cystoscopy and renal ultrasound. Persistent MH on repeat UA warrants an offer of evaluation appropriate to the patient’s risk.

document_sections.heading: Intermediate Risk
document_sections.content: Cystoscopy and renal ultrasound remain the recommended evaluation. For appropriately counseled patients who prefer to avoid cystoscopy and accept the risk of not directly viewing the bladder, clinicians may offer urine cytology or urine-based tumor markers (UBTMs). The rationale for limiting this option to intermediate risk is that test results can meaningfully alter posttest malignancy probability and management. The stated approximate cancer risk is 1% (0.2%3.1%); after a negative UBTM/cytology with high negative predictive value (NPV), the detection probability falls to 0.1% to 0.4%, comparable to low/negligible risk. The supporting studies included cohorts with MH patients constituting at least 25% and at least 100 MH patients. In a randomized trial comparing Cxbladder Triage–guided evaluation with routine cystoscopy, Cxbladder Triage had 99% NPV and the marker-guided approach reduced cystoscopy use by 59%. Other UBTMs and urine cytology reported NPV of 95% to 100% in the target population and are also options. An intermediate-risk patient who omits cystoscopy because of marker results should repeat UA within 12 months and undergo cystoscopy if MH remains. Benefit of these tests for deciding on cystoscopy has not been established in low/negligible- or high-risk patients, and the guideline recommends against that use. At low/negligible risk, the 0.0%-0.4% pretest probability makes a positive result likely to be false positive, potentially prompting unnecessary anxiety and evaluation. At high risk, a negative UBTM is not believed to lower the 1.3%-6.3% pretest probability enough to safely omit cystoscopy.

document_sections.heading: High Risk
document_sections.content: Although a large cohort study suggests low diagnostic yield for CT imaging, recent cohort studies report higher upper-tract cancer rates in high-risk MH. Multiphasic CT remains the gold-standard evaluation in this group because it visualizes renal parenchyma and urothelium. Absolute contraindications to CT urogram are described as very uncommon; newer studies report negligible contrast-induced nephropathy risk even with estimated glomerular filtration rate < 45. Following an appropriately risk-stratified negative evaluation, most patients do not need continuing urologic monitoring and can be discharged after shared decision-making informed by available evidence. Recent studies found that a history of MH did not raise subsequent cancer risk; later cancer diagnoses after a negative MH evaluation were negligible in frequency and occurred more than 3 years afterward. These findings should inform whether to repeat UA and its timing.

document_sections.heading: Key Takeaways
document_sections.content: The low/negligible designation reflects minimal malignancy risk and supports repeat UA instead of immediate investigation. Without other high-risk features, a woman must not be placed in the high-risk category solely because of age. UBTMs or cytology may further stratify intermediate-risk patients who wish to avoid cystoscopy, but should not determine the need for cystoscopy at low/negligible or high risk. After a negative MH evaluation, patients and clinicians should jointly decide whether and when to repeat UA.

document_sections.heading: Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: Highlights From the New AUA Guideline
document_sections.content: Some patients repeatedly receive antibiotics for diagnoses labeled prostatitis or epididymitis despite negative cultures and unchanged pain. Scrotal pain accounts for up to 2.5% of outpatient urology visits and 55 million health care dollars annually. A new AUA guideline addresses the evaluation and management of these patients.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Patients with NIH category III chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) can have perineal, testicular or penile pain, dysuria, or painful ejaculation. Pain associated with bladder filling and/or emptying instead suggests interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, addressed in a separate guideline. In the NIH-sponsored Multidisciplinary Approach to the Study of Chronic Pelvic Pain study, Lai et al found that men reporting pain during bladder filling or painful urgency, compared with men reporting neither, had more severe urological and generalized symptoms and poorer quality of life (QOL). Chronic scrotal content pain (CSCP) denotes unilateral orchialgia, whereas CPPS may combine scrotal pain with diffuse pain elsewhere, suggesting broader neuromuscular involvement rather than isolated testicular disease.

document_sections.heading: History and Review of Symptoms
document_sections.content: CP/CPPS and CSCP require exclusion of other pathology. History-taking should cover pain, urinary, sexual and bowel symptoms. Pelvic floor myalgia (PFM) or dysfunction is very common in CPPS, and painful ejaculation clearly indicates PFM. The Genitourinary Pain Index and Chronic Orchialgia Symptom Index may help assess CPPS and CSCP, respectively. Review should also consider irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome; a herniated vertebral disc can contribute neurologically, while hip or other musculoskeletal problems may accompany pain or PFM. Assessment of psychosocial health is important for therapeutic rapport: clinicians should communicate their understanding of symptoms, affirm the reality of the pain and acknowledge its effect on QOL. Coexisting anxiety, depression, adverse childhood experiences and previous sexual trauma should be addressed.

document_sections.content: The figure presents the diagnostic approach to male chronic pelvic pain.

document_sections.heading: Figure 2. Standardized male pelvic floor examination.
document_sections.content: The examination palpates pelvic floor muscles through the rectum with the patient either bending forward while facing down or lying on one side with bent knees. Tenderness is assessed in the posterior levator ani on each side at 1 and 11 o’clock, the anterior levator ani at 5 and 7 o’clock, and the lateral obturator internus at 3 and 9 o’clock. External palpation assesses the perineal body between the anus and scrotum at 6 o’clock. Part B depicts the muscles from inside the pelvis.

document_sections.heading: Physical Exam
document_sections.content: Examination should include focused neurological, abdominal, pelvic and genital assessments. External genital and scrotal examination seeks masses, induration, hydrocele, hernia and skin lesions. The 360 Digital Rectal Exam assesses prostate nodules, asymmetry and tenderness, and carefully identifies whether and where pelvic floor muscles are tender. The focused neurological assessment considers neurological causes, dermatomal pain distribution, posture and gait.

document_sections.heading: Workup
document_sections.content: Basic testing comprises urinalysis for microscopic hematuria and a mid-stream urine culture to exclude infection. Testicular ultrasound is optional and may be considered in CSCP when the diagnosis is unclear to exclude other pathology. Additional imaging, such as hip or spine imaging, should follow findings on neuromuscular examination.

document_sections.heading: Medications
document_sections.content: Oral α blockers are most suited to men who have both pain and obstructive voiding symptoms. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications are best included within multimodal care. Neuropathic-pain treatments include tricyclic antidepressant medications and either gabapentin or pregabalin. A reanalysis of previously negative pelvic-pain trials found a better response to the neuroleptic medications among patients stratified as having widespread rather than localized pelvic pain. An empirical 4- or 6-week antibiotic course is not recommended. For CP/CPPS, antibiotics should be used only with a positive culture; in chronic orchialgia, one short empirical course of 10days is reasonable. Daily tadalafil improves urinary symptoms and QOL in CPPS with or without erectile dysfunction and may lessen pain. The studied phytotherapeutics saw palmetto, quercetin and pollen extract may be useful.

document_sections.heading: Pelvic Floor Physical Therapy
document_sections.content: Referral to a physical therapist trained in pelvic floor care can be very helpful for men with PFM or abdominopelvic muscle myalgia. Within multimodal care, the therapist can help confirm the diagnosis and provide myofascial release and biofeedback to reduce resting pelvic muscle tone.

document_sections.heading: Stress Management
document_sections.content: Multimodal care involving psychiatrists for cognitive behavior therapy and stress-coping skills can limit symptom exacerbations. Guided meditation and diaphragmatic breathing are also useful relaxation methods.

document_sections.heading: Acupuncture
document_sections.content: Acupuncture has been examined in several studies. In a large multicenter sham-controlled trial in China, a reduction of ≥ 6 in total NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index occurred at week 8 and week 32 in 60.6% and 61.5% of men receiving acupuncture, respectively, versus sham-response rates of 36.8% and 38.3%. The trial showed a significant positive effect.

document_sections.heading: Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy
document_sections.content: A guideline meta-analysis considered 11 extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) trials. Studies outside the US using varied low-intensity ESWL techniques over 2 to 12 weeks reported improvement in the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index, pain and urinary symptoms. ESWL is not readily available, its use for CPPS remains off label, and further investigation is warranted.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Treatments for CSCP
document_sections.content: For isolated orchialgia, spermatic cord block provides diagnostic information: relief is temporary, but a strong response suggests possible benefit from microsurgical denervation of the spermatic cord (MSDSC). Across trials, complete or substantial pain relief after MSDSC ranges from 77% to 100%. Earlier MSDSC ligated all structures apart from the testicular artery and some lymphatic vessels. In spermatic-cord biopsies, Parekattil et al identified small-fiber Wallerian degeneration mainly in 3 sites: cremasteric muscle fibers, the peri-vasal sheath and posterior-cord lipomatous tissue. A targeted technique based on those findings divides those areas while retaining the vas deferens and lymphatic vessels. Expert opinion regards vasovasostomy and epididymectomy as remaining options for postvasectomy pain syndrome alongside MSDSC. Inguinal orchiectomy may be considered only as a last resort after conservative and less-invasive surgical options fail.

document_sections.heading: Summary
document_sections.content: The new guideline emphasizes comprehensive history and physical examination, multimodal treatment across a broad set of options, and attention to psychosocial factors. Repeated antibiotic treatment does not help.

document_sections.heading: Update on the SOUL Trial: To Stent or Not to Stent?
document_sections.content: The article describes the Stent Omission After Ureteroscopy and Lithotripsy (SOUL) trial, designed to compare outcomes after uncomplicated ureteroscopy with and without a temporary ureteral stent; its results were not yet presented.

document_sections.heading: The Problem
document_sections.content: Ureteroscopy is the most common US treatment procedure for upper urinary tract stones. A temporary postoperative ureteral stent can aid renal drainage and prevent pain due to ureteral injury or obstructing fragments, but can also cause morbidity. In Michigan Urological Surgery Improvement Collaborative (MUSIC) work, stent placement increased the odds of an emergency department visit after ureteroscopy by 25%. Many visits involved potentially modifiable pain, urinary discomfort or hematuria.

document_sections.heading: Is a Ureteral Stent Necessary After Ureteroscopy?
document_sections.content: AUA guidance permits stent omission after uncomplicated ureteroscopy, defined by absence of ureteric injury, normal contralateral kidney, no impaired renal function, no planned secondary ureteroscopy (stone size <1.5 cm), and no ureteral stricture or other anatomical obstacle to fragment clearance. Nevertheless, a stent is placed after ureteroscopy and stone intervention in approximately 80% of US cases.

document_sections.heading: Why Do Urologists Undertake Routine Stenting?
document_sections.content: Conflicting outcome evidence may contribute to limited stent omission. A 2019 Cochrane Review of 16 randomized clinical trials (RCTs) found that stenting might slightly reduce unplanned return visits, but judged this finding very uncertain. Evidence was also insufficient to support stenting as a means of reducing postoperative pain, narcotic use, UTI, readmission or strictures. The review called for larger, higher-quality trials.

document_sections.heading: What Does a High-Quality Trial Mean?
document_sections.content: Surgical trials face difficulties with patient-centered design and applicability to routine care because only a minority of patients accept randomization. Among MUSIC patient advocates, only 1 in 3 said they would accept assignment by chance in a future stent-omission trial. Failure to capture outcomes among those declining randomization creates selection bias and restricts generalizability. Many trials also do not systematically measure patient-reported outcomes, health-related quality of life or the full range of postintervention health care use.

document_sections.heading: What Is the Solution?
document_sections.content: MUSIC began SOUL on June 1, 2023. This single-blinded, pragmatic, multicenter study combines an RCT with an observational cohort to compare stent placement and omission after uncomplicated ureteroscopy for upper urinary tract stones. Its hypothesis is that omission improves health-related quality of life and 30-day health care utilization; these are proposed effects, not reported results. Interviews and surveys also examine patient and surgeon views and preferences about stenting. The co-primary outcomes are change in PROMIS Pain Interference scores at postoperative day 7 to 10 and unplanned health care use within 30 days of ureteroscopy. The eligibility table specifies enrollment criteria and intraoperative findings that preclude randomization.

document_sections.heading: Table. Eligibility Criteria for the Stent Omission After Ureteroscopy and Lithotripsy (SOUL) Clinical Trial
document_sections.content: The table lists inclusion and exclusion criteria for SOUL and complications identified at the end of ureteroscopy that make a patient ineligible for assignment to stent versus no stent.

document_sections.heading: SOUL Trial Workflow
document_sections.content: SOUL includes patients who accept randomization and patients who decline it; stent omission is the intervention because it occurs in a minority of current cases. In the randomized cohort, a web-based assignment to stent or no stent occurs intraoperatively after lithotripsy. Patients declining randomization can enter the observational cohort, in which the surgeon decides on stenting. All participants complete validated patient-reported surveys at 7 to 10 days and again at 4 to 6 weeks. Daily text-message assessments from postoperative day 1 through 10 ask about current pain, medication use and interference with activities. These real-time assessments in everyday surroundings are intended to reduce recall bias and improve tracking of symptoms; time away from work or school will also be recorded. The target is 792 patients over a 2-year period at 16 centers, comprising 264 randomized and 528 observational participants. As of March 25, 2025, enrollment was 534, including 204 (38%) in the randomized cohort.

document_sections.heading: How Can You Facilitate Stent Omission in Your Practice?
document_sections.content: Successful omission requires patient selection, counseling and care throughout the perioperative course. Described ideal candidates have not been prestented, have stones ≤ 10 mm at any location, and have not undergone mechanical ureteral dilation > 12F or use of a ureteral access sheath. Counseling helps establish expectations and postoperative symptom control. MUSIC has developed standardized education materials and multimodal pain-management pathways.

document_sections.heading: What Do We Hope to Achieve?
document_sections.content: SOUL aims to supply patient-centered evidence comparing stent placement and omission after uncomplicated ureteroscopy and to support shared decisions between patients and urologists. Its authors describe the anticipated contribution as dependent on successful completion of the study.

document_sections.heading: Panel Discussion: Do We Need to Do Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy Anymore?
document_sections.content: New aspiration technologies remove stone material by applying suction through modified access or visualization devices. The article considers 3 available classes: direct in-scope suction, flexible and navigable suction ureteral access sheaths, and steerable ureteroscopic renal evacuation.

document_sections.heading: Direct In-Scope Suction
document_sections.content: Direct in-scope suction (DISS) adds two 3-way stopcock adapters to the irrigation channel of a semirigid or flexible ureteroscope. One connects to wall or portable suction and the other to standard irrigation supplied by pressure bags or continuous systems. Alternating suction during or after laser lithotripsy extracts fragments or dust through the scope. Gauhar et al found DISS feasible, with an acceptable retreatment rate compared with suction ureteral access sheaths. In their comparison, retrograde intrarenal surgery using DISS was feasible for larger stones (median 22 mm vs 13 mm); operating time was longer with DISS, whereas hospital stays were shorter. The technique can be used across renal locations and during or after dusting; the authors describe it as a potentially cost-effective modification that may improve retrograde intrarenal surgery outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Flexible and Navigable Suction Ureteral Access Sheath
document_sections.content: The flexible and navigable (FANS) vacuum-assisted sheath can reach different calyces to remove fragments and dust directly. Huang et al reported significantly higher stone-free rates for vacuum-assisted dusting than for traditional flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy: immediately, 78.6% vs 50.5%; at follow-up, 94.2% vs 75.7%. Their findings extended across stone sizes, including 2- to 3-cm stones. Zeng et al described a modified sheath with an oblique suction-evacuation port and pressure regulation. Continuous removal of irrigation fluid and fragments produced a clearer view and might lower intrarenal pressure and, consequently, infectious complications. Further technological developments appear promising for complex stones that might otherwise require more invasive treatment.

document_sections.heading: Steerable Ureteroscopic Renal Evacuation
document_sections.content: Steerable ureteroscopic renal evacuation (SURE) uses the single-use CVAC System, integrating aspiration and ureteroscopy to navigate the renal collecting system. The original CVAC catheter had a separate ureteroscope, a 7F vacuum lumen and an 11.9F outer diameter. The second-generation device combines direct visualization, laser lithotripsy, microjet irrigation, dynamic suction and stone collection while retaining a separate 7F vacuum lumen. Dedicated irrigation and suction channels sustain simultaneous flow and remove dust and fragments up to 2.0 mm during and after lithotripsy. Its steering controls aid navigation; one operator can control on-demand irrigation and suction using connections compatible with standard operating-room equipment. Sur et al reported SURE to be safe, feasible and potentially more effective than basket extraction after laser lithotripsy, removing significantly more stone volume and a greater fraction of total stone volume. In Matlaga et al’s multicenter prospective randomized noninferiority ASPIRE study, SURE had noninferior stone-free rates versus standard ureteroscopy, with significantly better stone clearance (96.9% vs 92.9%) and less residual stone volume (14.3 mm³ vs 70.2 mm³). In Stern et al’s multi-institutional study, SURE treated large stone burdens (mean preoperative stone burden of 29 ± 12 mm), including patients receiving anticoagulation or living with neurological conditions. Stone clearance was 96.1%, and 91.7% of patients achieved > 90% clearance.

document_sections.heading: Comparison With Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy
document_sections.content: These aspiration techniques are less invasive than percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) and are described as reducing morbidity. PCNL treats large stone burdens but entails bleeding risk, possible injury to surrounding organs and longer hospital stays. In Stern et al’s SURE study, 90.5% of patients avoided previously planned staged procedures; clearance across stone sizes ranged from 93.8% to 98.9%, with no device-related complications or postoperative admissions. Huang et al reported an immediate stone-free rate of 57.1% with FANS for stones 2 to 3 cm. Although many guidelines retain PCNL as the gold standard for stones > 2 cm, aspiration methods may offer alternatives, particularly for patients poorly suited to PCNL because of anticoagulation, obesity, anatomical abnormalities or comorbidities. The authors suggest that further evidence could prompt reconsideration of traditional PCNL thresholds. DISS, FANS and SURE may reduce the need for PCNL in selected cases, but PCNL remains an essential option and further research is needed.

document_sections.heading: Area Deprivation Index and Distressed Communities Index and 24-Hour Urine Abnormalities
document_sections.content:
Kidney stones affect 10% of the US population, and approximately one-half of affected patients recur over a 10-year follow-up. Low socioeconomic status (SES) and social disadvantage have been linked to stone-related risks, including stone frequency, emergency-room imaging differences, more invasive or more frequent treatment, and stone size at percutaneous nephrolithotomy. Twenty-four-hour urine (24hU) measurements inform recurrence risk and medical prevention. Prior studies link low SES with calcinuria, hypocitraturia and low urinary potassium; disadvantage and food insecurity may also influence stone risk. SES is multifactorial, so income or insurance alone may not represent it well. Education and food-desert residence can be difficult to obtain and interpret at the bedside, while multivariable models need frequent updates and statistical support. Area Deprivation Index (ADI) is a publicly available, annually updated neighborhood SES measure funded by NIH. It uses 17 US Census variables linked to residential addresses and assigns neighborhood percentiles from 1 to 100, with 100 indicating greatest disadvantage; it can identify clusters of higher-risk neighborhoods. The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation incorporated ADI into ACO Reach. Distressed Communities Index (DCI) is another SES measure, based on 7 variables at zip-code level. Both offer accessible approximations of SES and can be integrated into medical records. Earlier work associated ADI- and DCI-measured SES with low urine volume and hypocitraturia, but whether they identify distinct 24hU abnormalities or differ in association strength was uncertain. The authors therefore compared ADI, DCI and 24hU associations in a single-institution, multihospital retrospective study of adults undergoing percutaneous nephrolithotomy over a 5-year period. They linked residential locations and zip codes to national index scores and examined demographics, 24hU findings, stone composition and medical pharmacotherapy.

For both ADI and DCI, the most disadvantaged quartiles were associated with younger age, higher BMI, non-White race and lower likelihood of completing 24hU testing. The most disadvantaged quartile under either index also had significantly greater risk of low urine volume and calcium phosphate stone composition. Higher ADI, but not DCI, was associated with hypocitraturia. Under DCI, greater neighborhood disadvantage was linked to lower urinary uric acid and oxalate; better SES was associated with greater risk of hyperuricosuria and hyperoxaluria. Associations remained significant in multivariable analysis. Where both indices’ models were significant for a 24hU measure, neither fitted better. Thus, the indices identify different associations without an overall difference in predictive ability. Either may help identify patients with higher-risk 24hU parameters; access, record-system integration and geography may guide the choice. The authors propose that SES-related urinary patterns could help investigate community-level causes. They note that foods rich in oxalate include nuts, berries and greens; fruit and vegetable intake relates to urinary citrate, and high-protein diets can increase uric acid excretion. Such foods may cost more or be inaccessible in food deserts, and physical labor may increase water loss and lower urine output. Identifying stone formers with lower SES may create prevention opportunities; future targeted-intervention research is needed to address socioeconomic barriers.

document_sections.heading: Testosterone Supplementation After Localized Prostate Cancer: The Current State of the Literature
document_sections.content: Testosterone therapy (TTh) was long regarded as contraindicated after prostate cancer, partly because work from the 1940s showed regression after castration. More recent evidence challenges an assumption that TTh inevitably causes recurrence. Morgentaler and colleagues’ saturation model proposes that prostate cancer cells respond to testosterone only at very low concentrations and that additional testosterone after androgen-receptor saturation does not accelerate growth. The model prompted reassessment of TTh risk. Newer studies also report no apparent increase in prostate cancer incidence with TTh among men without prior cancer. A retrospective study of 5199 men after radical prostatectomy for localized disease found no evidence that TTh caused biochemical recurrence (BCR); the association with lower BCR risk was nonsignificant (HR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.48-1.46). Its estimated 5-year BCR probability was less than 2% in both treated and untreated groups. Earlier studies likewise reported higher testosterone without increased PSA after prostatectomy. Pastuszak et al compared 103 hypogonadal men receiving TTh after prostatectomy with 49 nonhypogonadal reference patients and observed 4 versus 8 recurrences, despite significantly increased testosterone in the treated group. A US Veterans Affairs analysis of 69,984 patients diagnosed from 2001 to 2015 and treated with surgery or radiation found no increased BCR, prostate cancer–specific mortality or overall mortality with TTh after definitive treatment.

document_sections.heading: TESTOSTERONE SUPPLEMENTATION AFTER LOCALIZED PROSTATE CANCER
document_sections.content: In Applewhite et al’s retrospective study of 43 men receiving active surveillance (AS) for low-risk prostate cancer, PSA did not change significantly after TTh initiation (P = .87), and biopsy progression was comparable to that in the broader AS population. Of 15 men who underwent repeat biopsy, 80% had no progression and 3 developed Gleason 7 disease during extended follow-up (mean: 79.5 months); none developed metastases. These findings suggest TTh may be used safely in carefully selected AS patients without a significant rise in progression risk. After definitive prostate cancer treatment, decisions about TTh should be individualized, with regular monitoring of PSA velocity and testosterone. Potential improvements in energy, sexual function, bone density, body composition and possibly cardiovascular health must be balanced against the theoretical possibility of stimulating occult cancer cells. Available evidence suggests carefully selected men can receive TTh after definitive treatment for localized disease, with stronger evidence after prostatectomy. Larger prospective studies and longer follow-up would strengthen these conclusions; clinicians should discuss the evidence and monitor carefully.

document_sections.heading: Current State of Intravesical Therapies for NonmuscleInvasive Bladder Cancer
document_sections.content: Newer treatments for nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) include immunotherapy, gene therapy and sustained intravesical drug delivery. The article reviews clinical findings for investigational and recently Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–approved treatments.

document_sections.heading: Nadofaragene Firadenovec
document_sections.content: Nadofaragene firadenovec is an intravesical gene therapy using a nonreplicating adenovirus to deliver the interferon alfa-2b gene to bladder urothelium. FDA approval in 2022 followed a phase 3 study in bacillus CalmetteGuérin (BCG)–unresponsive highrisk (HR) NMIBC with carcinoma in situ (CIS) with or without papillary disease. Among patients with CIS, complete response (CR) at any time was 55%, median CR duration was 9.7 months, and 24% remained free of recurrence at 12 months. In papillary-only disease, CR was 72.9%, with median duration of 12.3 months. High-grade (HG) recurrence-free survival (RFS) at 12 months was 43.8%; among patients without recurrence at 3 months, 60% remained recurrence-free at 12 months. Unlike other trials discussed, this trial did not offer reinduction to initial nonresponders. Longer-term HG RFS at 24, 36, 48 and 57 months was 36.4%, 25.5%, 20.0% and 10.9%, respectively. Five-year cystectomy-free survival was 43.2% for CIS and 58.7% for papillary disease. ABLE-22 is studying combinations with chemo-/immunotherapy in HG BCG-unresponsive disease, and ABLE-32 compares nadofaragene with observation in intermediate-risk (IR) disease.

document_sections.heading: Nogapendekin Alfa-Inbakicept + BCG
document_sections.content: Nogapendekin alfa-inbakicept, an IL-15 receptor agonist, activates natural killer and CD8+ T cells and is administered with BCG to enhance immune response. QUILT 3.032 preceded FDA approval in April 2024. In cohort A, which included CIS with or without papillary disease, CR was 55%, 56%, 45% and 33% at 3, 6, 12 and 18 months, respectively; median CR duration was 26.6 months. Baseline-disease CR rates were 68% for CIS only, 81% for CIS + Ta and 67% for CIS + T1. Among patients reinduced after lacking CR at 3 months, 54% later achieved CR. At 24 months, cystectomy-free survival was 89.2% among responders and 63.2% among nonresponders. In papillary-only cohort B, median disease-free survival (DFS) was 19.3 months and 24-month DFS was 48.3%. Monotherapy cohort C closed for futility.

document_sections.heading: Cretostimogene Grenadenorepvec
document_sections.content: Cretostimogene grenadenorepvec (CG0070) is an oncolytic adenovirus directed at tumor cells with defective Rb signaling and expresses granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor. An AUA2025 update of BOND003 cohort C in BCG-refractory CIS with or without Ta/T1 reported overall CR of 75.5%; 50% of patients receiving repeat induction converted to CR. CR rates were 46.4% at 12 months and 33.7% at 24 months; median response duration was 27.9 months and ongoing. There were no grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events (AEs). Overall, 95% received all protocol treatments and none discontinued because of treatment. Early data from cohort P, limited to HG Ta/T1, showed 90.5% HG RFS at 3 and 9 months. PIVOT-006 is a phase 3 comparison with surveillance in IR NMIBC; CORE-008 is a phase 2 investigation in BCG-naïve and BCG-exposed HG disease.

document_sections.heading: TAR-200
document_sections.content: TAR-200 is inserted into the bladder through a urethral catheter and releases gemcitabine over weeks. In SunRISe-1, cohort 1 receiving TAR-200 + cetrelimab had 67.9% CR and 26% discontinuation. Cohort 2 receiving TAR-200 alone had 82.8% CR at 12 weeks; estimated CR was 75.7% at 6 months and 61.9% at 12 months. At a median 30-week follow-up, 85% of responses persisted. Cetrelimab-only cohort 3 had 46.4% CR and 23% discontinuation. In papillary-only cohort 4, which included ~40% T1, DFS was 85.3% at 6 months and 81.1% at 9 months; 7.7% discontinued because of AEs. SunRISe-3 compares TAR-200 with or without cetrelimab against BCG in BCG-naïve HR NMIBC. SunRISe-5 compares TAR-200 against investigator-selected chemotherapy in BCG-unresponsive papillary-only disease.

document_sections.heading: TAR-210
document_sections.content: TAR-210 uses the TAR-200 delivery platform to administer erdafitinib, a pan-FGFR inhibitor, directly into the bladder for FGFR3-mutant NMIBC. MoonRISE-1 began in April 2024 and compares TAR-210 given every-3months with intravesical chemotherapy in IR NMIBC. Preliminary findings showed 90% CR at 3 months, with 89% durable response at 9 months.

It identifies which listed treatments have FDA approval.

document_sections.heading: Sasanlimab
document_sections.content: Sasanlimab is a subcutaneous anti-PD-1 antibody that produces systemic immune activation. In the AUA2025 presentation of the CREST III trial in BCG-naïve HR NMIBC, event-free survival (EFS) with BCG + sasanlimab was 84.7% at 12 months and 82.1% at 24 months, compared with 79.9% and 74.8%, respectively, with BCG alone. The reported sasanlimab-arm findings included a 32% reduction in 24-month EFS and a 50% reduction in HG recurrence. Treatment completion was 46.3% with BCG + sasanlimab versus 57.8% with BCG alone. In the CIS-only subgroup, 36-month EFS was 92%. The findings also underscored the importance of BCG maintenance in this population.

document_sections.heading: Detalimogene Voraplasmid
document_sections.content: EG-70 (detalimogene voraplasmid) is a nonviral, nonintegrating intravesical immunotherapy designed to provoke a local antitumor immune response. The phase 1/2 LEGEND study investigates it in BCG-refractory and BCG-exposed NMIBC with CIS. Phase 2 CR rates were 70% at 3 months and 60% at 6 months. Most reported treatment-related AEs were grade 1 to 2 and were consistent with catheterization and instillation.

document_sections.heading: TARA-002
document_sections.content: TARA-002 is an investigational immune-stimulating agent derived from OK-432, an inactivated Streptococcus pyogenes preparation. It is being studied in both BCG-unresponsive and BCG-naïve NMIBC. In phase 1, CR at 3 months was 43% overall and 63% for CIS-only disease. The phase 2 ADVANCED-2 study assesses induction followed by maintenance over 15 months. No grade ≥ 3 treatment-related AEs were reported.

document_sections.heading: Gemcitabine/Docetaxel
document_sections.content: Sequential intravesical gemcitabine/docetaxel (Gem/Doce) is an available alternative for BCG-unresponsive bladder cancer. Previous nonrandomized series in BCG-unresponsive CIS reported RFS of 60% at 1 year and 50% at 2 years; a 5-year RFS of 28% was also reported for BCG-unresponsive patients. A more recent analysis found HG RFS of 63%, 47% and 38% at 1-, 2- and 5-year follow-up, respectively. In a small prospective study of BCG-naïve HR NMIBC, CR was 100% at 3 months and RFS was 92% at 12 months. The randomized phase 3 BRIDGE trial is comparing Gem/Doce against BCG for BCG-naïve HG disease.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: Emerging NMIBC treatments aim to improve effectiveness, durability and patient experience while retaining the bladder. Investigational approaches include multiple immunotherapies, combinations with BCG, and treatment of BCG-naïve or IR disease. More mature data are needed to establish whether they delay recurrence and progression. Longer-term cystectomy-free outcomes and pathological findings at cystectomy are needed to substantiate a stepwise approach using multiple agents.
